subject: Site safety of the current page (who is responsible, whether it impersonates another party, what it is for, whether a pitch is disclosed) and, when the page is one piece of writing, scrutiny of that writing. A listing is not an article. A purpose of opinion is not a safety failure. The report is evidence, not a reputation score for a familiar site.

questions.instructions: From the hostname, title, siteName, author, and visible text, can a reader name a real publisher, organization, or person responsible for this page? The author and siteName fields are page chrome: byline, publisher name, author link, JSON-LD, or metadata. They count even when those strings were stripped from the main body text as navigation. A publishing platform plus a named author or public handle is identifiable. A brand-like word in a headline, a generic desk name, the host alone, or the word official with no named party is not. Judge whether a party can be named from this page. Do not treat a well-known host as identified, and do not require a contact address.

criteria.true: A specific organization, publication, platform-plus-author, or named person is identifiable as responsible.
criteria.false: The responsible party is missing, anonymous, only a generic label, or only a slogan that names no publisher.

questions.instructions: Does the visible branding, title, and claimed publisher match the actual hostname, or does the page impersonate another party? Judge identity fraud, not writing quality or fame. A site speaking as itself is honest, including a harsh critic of a named institution. A page that copies another organization's name, logo, or login while living on a different host is not. Lookalike spelling of another party's host is impersonation. Satire that clearly labels itself as satire is honest about identity.

criteria.true: The branding matches the hostname, or a hosting platform is presenting a named author's page as that author's page.
criteria.false: The page claims to be a different organization than the hostname suggests (typosquat, fake login, copied masthead, spoofed institution).

questions.instructions: What is the primary purpose of this page, given pageKind, the title, and the visible text? pageKind is a structural label from the client: portal means a listing of destinations, article means one piece of writing. Do not use the host's reputation. Purpose is not a popularity or quality score. Opinion, teaching, and commentary are opinion_analysis. A page that looks like reporting but exists to sell, rank products, or capture a lead is commercial. Incompatible purposes mixed without labeling them are unclear.

criteria.news_reference: Reports or explains events or facts in a journalistic or encyclopedic way.
criteria.opinion_analysis: Argues a position, teaches, or interprets; the author's view or experience is the point.
criteria.portal: A listing, index, or headline board rather than one piece of writing.
criteria.commercial: Exists mainly to sell a product, service, or lead, including affiliate copy dressed as reporting.
criteria.satire_entertainment: Humor, fiction, or entertainment that is not claiming to be a news report.
criteria.unclear: Purpose cannot be determined, or incompatible purposes are mixed without labeling them.

questions.instructions: If the page is trying to sell something, raise money, or advocate for a party that would benefit, which of these is true? no_pitch means there is no sales or advocacy pitch. named_beneficiary means a pitch is present and the beneficiary or sponsor is named. hidden_beneficiary means the page pushes a product, donation, or political outcome while hiding who benefits. An obvious storefront is no_pitch. Naming a product is not named_beneficiary when the reader cannot tell who is paid to promote it.

criteria.no_pitch: There is no sales or advocacy pitch.
criteria.named_beneficiary: A pitch is present and the beneficiary or sponsor is named.
criteria.hidden_beneficiary: The page pushes a product, donation, or political outcome while hiding who benefits.

questions.instructions: How well does the visible text support the factual claims it presents as established? Count only evidence the reader can inspect on this page: named sources, data, documents, methods, or work the author presents as their own and points to. Design proposals, working hypotheses, and points the text marks as unverified, as needing an experiment, or as not yet measured are not established factual claims. Do not score a clearly marked proposal the same as an unsupported news assertion. Missing official links or measurements on a proposal still stay below the top of the rubric. Experts say with no name, and empty marketing claims, score low. Do not require a particular citation style. Do not credit a claim because the host is well known.
criteria: Established factual claims are made with little or no supporting evidence, data, or sources on the page.
Some established claims have sources or data, or the writing is a proposal or hypothesis whose main particulars are not checkable; important established claims or measurements are still missing.
The main factual claims presented as established are backed by named sources, data, documents, or the author's inspectable work.

questions.instructions: Does the text keep factual statements and the author's judgments distinct enough that a reader can tell them apart? An essay or opinion page may mix them; pass if judgments are readable as judgments and reported facts are not invented. Do not fail an essay for having a thesis. A speculative design marked as speculative, as a hypothesis, or as needing an experiment is not a judgment written as a measured fact. Fail when a judgment is written as a measured fact, or a measured fact is written as mere taste to dodge a source.

criteria.true: Facts and judgments are labeled or clearly separated, or the page is clearly an essay or opinion throughout.
criteria.false: Opinions are written as if they were established facts, or facts are framed as mere opinion to dodge responsibility.

questions.instructions: Does the text present specific numbers, dates, quotes, or named events as established external facts without a source the reader can check? The author's own stated work counts as a source when the page says it is theirs and gives a way to inspect it. A load-bearing particular given as external fact with no checkable source does not. Particulars the text marks as hypothesis, unverified, or needing an experiment are not unsourced facts; if those particulars still function as the main load-bearing numbers without a checkable source, choose some, not many. Round promotional figures (overnight, 10x, clinically proven with no study) count as specifics when they carry the claim as established fact.

criteria.none: Specific facts are sourced, are the author's own stated work, are marked as unverified hypothesis, or the page stays at a level of generality that does not invent particulars.
criteria.some: A few specifics lack a source, including unmeasured proposal details, but they are not presented as settled external facts that carry the piece.
criteria.many: Load-bearing numbers, dates, quotes, or events are given as established fact with no checkable source and are not the author's own stated work.

questions.instructions: Is the text free of internal contradictions on the same fact? Two statements that agree pass. Rhetorical repetition of the same claim is not a contradiction. Two incompatible numbers, dates, or outcomes for the same fact fail, as does a claim later denied as if it were never made.

criteria.true: No two statements conflict on the same fact.
criteria.false: The page states one thing and later the opposite, for example two different values for the same quantity.

questions.instructions: Does the text match how certain it sounds to the evidence it actually shows? Strong claims need strong evidence. Personal results marked as personal, and uncertain points that are hedged, pass. Claims marked as a hypothesis, as unverified, or as needing an experiment are correctly uncertain; do not treat them as settled facts. Health, money, identity, or law claims that sound settled need settled evidence on the page. Contested or thinly supported claims stated as settled fact fail.

criteria.true: Strong claims come with strong evidence; uncertain points are hedged or marked as the author's view, as a hypothesis, as unverified, or as unknown.
criteria.false: The page states contested or thinly supported claims as settled fact, or hides strong evidence behind false uncertainty.

questions.instructions: Sentences cut from this page are labeled s1, s2, and so on. The description of each label is that sentence. Choose the one sentence that bears on evidence for an established factual claim: a named source, a document, data, a method, or work the author presents as their own. Do not choose a sentence merely because it is the most specific paragraph on the page. Choose none only when no labeled sentence bears on that evidence. If the writing fails this question, choose the sentence that causes the failure, not a sentence that only supports a passing part of the page. Do not write a new sentence.

criteria.none: No single sentence carries this question.

questions.instructions: Sentences cut from this page are labeled s1, s2, and so on. The description of each label is that sentence. Choose the one sentence that bears on separating fact and opinion: a fact beside the author's judgment, a judgment written as a measured fact, or a measured fact written as mere taste. Do not choose a sentence merely because it states a number or a source. Choose none only when no labeled sentence bears on that separation. If the writing fails this question, choose the sentence that causes the failure, not a sentence that only supports a passing part of the page. Do not write a new sentence.

criteria.none: No single sentence carries this question.

questions.instructions: Sentences cut from this page are labeled s1, s2, and so on. The description of each label is that sentence. Choose the one sentence that bears on a specific number, date, quotation, or named event. Prefer a particular given as established fact without a checkable source when one is present; otherwise the sentence that holds the load-bearing particular. Do not choose a sentence that only names a source and contains no particular. Choose none only when no labeled sentence bears on a particular. If the writing fails this question, choose the sentence that causes the failure, not a sentence that only supports a passing part of the page. Do not write a new sentence.

criteria.none: No single sentence carries this question.

questions.instructions: Sentences cut from this page are labeled s1, s2, and so on. The description of each label is that sentence. Choose the one sentence that bears on internal consistency: a number, date, or outcome that conflicts with another sentence on the same fact, or a claim the page later takes back. If nothing conflicts, choose the sentence that states a fact another sentence also states. Do not choose a sentence only because it is the most concrete paragraph. Choose none only when no labeled sentence is about the same fact as another. If the writing fails this question, choose the sentence that causes the failure, not a sentence that only supports a passing part of the page. Do not write a new sentence.

criteria.none: No single sentence carries this question.

questions.instructions: Sentences cut from this page are labeled s1, s2, and so on. The description of each label is that sentence. Choose the one sentence whose certainty bears on this question: settled wording, a hedge, a hypothesis, or a personal result. Prefer the sentence where the strength of the wording and the evidence in it come apart, when one does. Do not choose a sentence only because it contains a number. Choose none only when no labeled sentence's certainty is at issue. If the writing fails this question, choose the sentence that causes the failure, not a sentence that only supports a passing part of the page. Do not write a new sentence.

criteria.none: No single sentence carries this question.
